If the prongs stay parallel the board is stress free; if they curve inward and pinch together, it is casehardened; prongs curving outward indicate the rarer reverse condition. Commercial kilns fix casehardening at the end of the schedule by conditioning: a deliberate spell of high humidity, often with live steam, that re-wets the shell slightly and relieves the set. If the shell tension set is severe and the core, still wet, is then dried too hard, the core itself can fail internally in tension, tearing along the rays in hidden slit-like voids. This is honeycomb, the worst drying defect, invisible until a saw or a moulder opens the board and reveals an interior like torn paper; it cannot be repaired, and thick oak dried in a hurry is its classic victim. The practical defences follow from the mechanism. Dry gently through the danger zone above the fibre saturation point, protect end grain, and keep thick stock out of aggressive kilns; when buying, prong-test a sample from any pallet of kiln-dried hardwood, and be suspicious of thick stock offered dry at improbable speed or price. When resawing any thick dried board into thinner leaves, expect movement, take equal amounts from both faces where possible, cut oversize, and let the halves settle for days and re-equilibrate before final machining, because even well-dried wood retains modest stress and fresh surfaces hold different moisture than the old ones.

sections.heading: Wane, Reaction Wood, Pitch Pockets and Warp
sections.body: Beyond the big three, a family of lesser defects appears constantly in the yard and deserves quick, confident recognition. Wane is the simplest: the presence of the original rounded surface of the log, with or without bark, along an edge of a board, because the sawyer cut too close to the outside. It costs bearing area and nailing edge rather than strength within the remaining wood, and grading rules cap how much of an edge may be waney; in rustic furniture the same feature is sold, at a premium, as a live edge. Pitch pockets are lens-shaped voids between growth rings filled with liquid or crystallised resin, common in spruce, pine and Douglas fir, usually the scar of cambium damage or wind flexing; small ones are cosmetic, but a deep pocket weeps resin through finishes for years and a row of them hints at a wind-shaken tree. Bark pockets are the equivalent with included bark. More consequential is reaction wood, the abnormal tissue a leaning tree builds to right itself, in two opposite forms. Conifers build compression wood on the underside of a lean: wide-ringed, dull, lifeless-looking wood, often forming an off-centre pith, that is brittle, weak for its weight, and above all shrinks along the grain up to ten or twenty times more than normal wood. Because normal longitudinal shrinkage is nearly zero, a board with a streak of compression wood on one edge bows and springs violently as it dries and can keep moving for years; it also breaks suddenly across the grain, which is why grading rules for ladder stock and scaffold planks specifically exclude it. Hardwoods do the opposite, building tension wood on the upper side of the lean; it is gelatinous in texture, planes and sands to a woolly, fuzzy surface that will not take a crisp finish, and likewise shows abnormal longitudinal shrinkage. Both forms betray themselves by an off-centre pith on the end grain and by rings markedly wider on one side than the other. Finally there is warp, the umbrella term for shape error, with four named components that can occur separately or together. Bow is curvature along the length seen from the side; spring or crook is curvature along the length seen from the face, the enemy of straight edges; cup is curvature across the width, the natural fate of flatsawn boards drying with the two-to-one tangential-to-radial shrinkage ratio; and twist is the propeller condition, where the four corners will not sit in one plane, commonly born of spiral grain in the tree. Small amounts of bow and spring are removed by jointing at the cost of thickness and width; cup is flattened by ripping wide boards into narrower ones before jointing; but twist wastes more wood than any other warp, and a badly twisted or sprung board is usually best crosscut into short lengths, within which the error becomes trivial.

sections.heading: Biological Defects: Fungi and Insects
sections.body: Two thresholds organise everything about decay. Wood-destroying fungi need moisture and cannot attack wood kept below about 20 percent moisture content, a figure comfortably above the 8 to 14 percent of any heated or ventilated interior; and they need oxygen, which is why wood permanently submerged, like foundation piles under the water table, lasts for centuries. Decay is therefore not a property of old wood but of wet wood, and every rotten sill, joist end or fence post is a moisture problem before it is a fungus problem. The attack comes in recognisable forms. Brown rots consume the cellulose and leave the brown lignin skeleton, shrinking the wood into the characteristic cubical cracked pattern of dry rot and quickly destroying strength; the name dry rot for Serpula lacrymans is a misnomer worth correcting, since the fungus needs moisture to start, though it can then conduct water through its own strands to colonise adjacent dry wood, which is what makes it uniquely dangerous in buildings. White rots consume lignin and cellulose together, leaving pale, stringy, spongy wood, and are commoner in hardwoods. Soft rot roughens chronically wet surfaces like cooling towers and ground-line posts. Critically, strength is lost before decay is clearly visible: wood in the early, incipient stage, called dote or doze, can have lost a third or more of its toughness while showing only faint discolouration. The field test is the pick test: pry up a splinter with an awl; sound wood breaks out in a long fibrous splinter, decayed wood breaks brashly, straight across, with little resistance. Not all fungal marks matter equally. Blue stain or sap stain, a blue-grey discolouration of softwood sapwood, is a pigmented mould living on cell contents, not cell walls; it costs appearance grade but essentially no strength, and the related black-line spalting prized by woodturners is partial decay caught, ideally, before softening. Insects divide by habitat. Powderpost beetles of the Lyctus group attack only the sapwood of coarse-pored hardwoods such as oak and ash, packing tunnels with flour-fine dust; the common furniture beetle, the woodworm of old pine furniture, leaves 1.5 to 2 millimetre exit holes and gritty pellets; the house longhorn beetle mines softwood roof timbers and can be structurally devastating; termites, where they occur, consume wood from within, leaving a painted shell, and warrant professional attention rather than improvisation. Two field rules keep buyers out of most trouble. First, fresh activity shows as clean, pale exit holes and new dust; old, dark, empty holes in bone-dry wood are usually history, since most borers need the higher moisture of unseasoned or damp wood, though Lyctus and furniture beetle can reinfest dry sapwood. Second, sapwood is the vulnerable band in nearly every species: a board of durable heartwood with a strip of sapwood along one edge is durable except exactly there, and outdoors that strip should be cut off or treated, not hoped over.

sections.heading: Grading: How Defects Are Measured and Priced
sections.body: Grading is the institutional machinery that turns a visual inspection of defects into a number an engineer or buyer can use, and it comes in two great families. Appearance grading, used for hardwoods destined for furniture and joinery, asks how much clear, defect-free wood can be cut from a board. The rules of the National Hardwood Lumber Association, which govern the North American trade and influence practice worldwide, define the top grade FAS, historically Firsts and Seconds, essentially as boards of a minimum size yielding at least 83 and one third percent clear cuttings of specified sizes; the successive grades, Select, Number 1 Common, Number 2 Common and below, admit smaller and fewer clear cuttings, roughly two thirds for Number 1 Common. The crucial insight for a buyer is that a lower grade is not worse wood but smaller patches of the same clear wood interrupted by more defects; a maker of small components can often buy Number 1 Common at a large discount and cut around the knots to obtain identical material to FAS. Structural grading, used for softwood construction timber, instead asks how much strength the defects have removed from the piece as a whole. Visual structural grading, under standards such as BS 4978 in Britain or the National Grading Rule species rules in North America, has a trained grader assess each piece in seconds: knot sizes are measured by projection and expressed as a knot area ratio, the fraction of the cross-section occupied by knots at the worst point; a margin condition records whether more than half of the outer quarters of the section is occupied; slope of grain is limited, commonly to about 1 in 6 for lower grades and 1 in 10 or better for higher ones; and fissures, wane, distortion, resin pockets and decay each have caps. The piece is then stamped, for example GS or SS in the British system, and those visual grades map to strength classes, C16 or C24 for typical European softwood, whose design stresses engineers take from tables. Because visual grading must assume the worst about what it cannot see, it is conservative, and machine strength grading has largely supplemented it for high volumes: a machine flexes each board or measures its acoustic stiffness, exploiting the strong statistical correlation between stiffness and strength, and stamps a class accordingly, catching good-but-knotty and poor-but-clear pieces that fool the eye. Three practical warnings complete the picture. A grade stamp applies to the whole piece as graded; crosscutting can upgrade it, but ripping a graded joist into two thinner ones voids the stamp, since the defect geometry changes. Grade describes the piece at grading, not after decades of wetting. And grading is statistical: design stresses are set low enough that the fifth-percentile piece is safe, which is why regraded, reclaimed or ungraded timber in structural positions requires either an engineer's judgement or generous, honest oversizing.

sections.heading: Reading a Board: Selection and Cutting Strategy
sections.body: Everything above condenses, at the timber rack, into a five-minute inspection routine that repays itself on every purchase. Start at the ends, because the end grain is the board's confession. Ring curvature tells you whether the piece is flatsawn, with rings running roughly parallel to the wide face and maximum movement across the width, or quartersawn, with rings standing upright and half the movement; the position of the heart, if present, predicts cupping and juvenile-wood misbehaviour; dark curved or radial lines warn of shake; and end splits show you immediately how much length to write off. Next sight along both edges from one end, like sighting a rifle, which reveals bow, spring and twist far better than any straightedge laid flat; reject or heavily discount twist. Scan the faces for knots and classify them as you look: tight, intergrown knots that will stay put, or encased knots ringed with bark and loose plugs that will not, and note whether any spike knots run into the edges. Look for the dull, lifeless stripe of compression wood in softwood, for woolly patches in hardwood that betray tension wood, for pitch pockets, wane, insect holes and the grey of sapwood in a species where sapwood matters. Check moisture if anything structural or fine depends on it: a resistance meter pushed into the face should read within a few points of the equilibrium value for the wood's destination, roughly 8 to 10 percent for centrally heated interiors, 12 to 16 for outdoors under cover, and readings that differ sharply between shell and core, if the meter has insulated pins, warn of a wet centre or locked-in stress. Then buy deliberately more than the cutting list demands; experienced makers allow 20 to 30 percent extra for clear work in knotty species, more in low grades, because defect waste is a certainty, not a risk. The cutting strategy that follows is the craft of getting high-grade results from mid-grade wood. Crosscut first, freeing the cutting-list lengths from around the defects rather than ripping full length and hoping; dock end splits generously, cutting 50 millimetres beyond the visible end of the crack, because checks run further than they show. Place what remains: knots into internal, hidden or low-stress components, never into joints; the straightest, most vertical grain into legs, rails and anything that must stay straight; pith and juvenile wood into nothing that matters. For structural work the same logic becomes rule rather than art: bearing ends must be free of wane and rot, notches and bored holes must avoid knots and stay out of the tension edge, and a joist with a large edge knot can often simply be turned so the knot sits in the compression zone or crowned so its camber works with the load. Reading wood this way is not lore; it is applied mechanism, and after a few hundred boards it becomes as fast as looking.

sections.heading: Prevention, Repair and Knowing When to Reject
sections.body: Defect management begins the day the tree is felled. Logs left in the sun split from the ends within days, so mills seal log ends with wax emulsion and convert quickly; the same wax, or thick paint in an emergency, belongs on the end grain of every freshly sawn board within hours of cutting. Air drying is a discipline of geometry: boards stacked flat on level bearers, separated by uniform stickers of dry wood about 20 to 25 millimetres square placed in vertical lines every 400 to 600 millimetres, the whole pile roofed against sun and rain, its top weighted so the upper boards cannot warp, and the ends of the pile shaded, since sun on end grain is the great splitter. The classical pace is a year of air drying per inch of thickness down to outdoor equilibrium, followed, for furniture stock, by weeks of acclimatisation indoors or a gentle kiln finish to interior moisture levels; hurrying past either stage is how checks and casehardening are bought. In service, prevention is mostly moisture management: keep structural timber below 20 percent by ventilation and detailing so decay never starts, prime the end grain of every exterior component, and expect and design for seasonal movement rather than fighting it, which is the entire logic of frame-and-panel construction. When defects have already happened, repair is often honest and durable. A check or split that has stopped moving can be stabilised with a butterfly key, the bowtie-shaped inlay of contrasting hardwood set across the crack that Japanese and studio furniture makers have made a signature; cut the recess so the key's grain runs across the split and it mechanically stitches the two sides together. Epoxy resin, tinted or filled, consolidates checks and knot holes in tabletops and turnery; thin cyanoacrylate locks small loose knots; and a knot in painted joinery can be bored out entirely and replaced with a glued cross-grain plug. What repair cannot honestly do is restore strength across a structural fracture: a filled check is cosmetic, and a beam that has split at a bearing or sheared along a shake needs sistering, replacement or an engineer, not adhesive. Finally, the reject list, the cases where the correct decision is to walk away or saw the piece into firewood lengths regardless of price. Reject for structural use: ring shake anywhere, compression failures across the grain, active decay or any wood that fails the splinter pick test, large knots or knot clusters at the tension edge that exceed the relevant grade, and casehardened stock destined for ripping. Reject for fine work: twist beyond what thicknessing can afford, compression wood, honeycomb, and boards whose defects sit exactly where the design needs its joints. A defective board is only a bargain when its defects fall where the work does not; the whole craft of this subject is knowing, before money changes hands, whether they do.

guides.safetyNote: Never machine, rip or turn timber containing loose knots, ring shake, deep checks or suspected internal splits at full speed: pieces can detach or the stock can burst apart. Inspect both faces and both ends first, tap turning blanks for dead sounds, wear eye and face protection at machines, and reject decayed or shake-ridden wood for any load-bearing use.

guides.title: Reading Wood Grain, Figure and Runout
guides.summary: How to read a board: the cell structure behind grain, what growth rings and rays reveal, how to identify figure, and how to spot runout and grain direction so that wood is cut, planed, bent and joined with its structure rather than against it.

sections.heading: Why Reading a Board Is the First Skill
sections.body: Wood is the only common structural material that arrives already organised. Steel is isotropic, meaning it behaves the same in every direction, and a woodworker coming from metal or plastic has to unlearn that assumption completely. A piece of timber is a bundle of long hollow cells glued together, laid down by a tree that was solving its own problems: standing up, carrying water from root to leaf, and resisting wind. Every property that matters in the workshop follows from that arrangement. Timber is roughly twenty to forty times stronger in tension along the fibres than across them, splits readily in one plane and hardly at all in another, moves a great deal in width and almost not at all in length as humidity changes, and cuts cleanly in one direction while tearing in the other. Reading a board means inferring that internal arrangement from what is visible on its faces and ends, and then making every subsequent decision, which face to plane first, which way to feed it, where a joint can go, whether it will do as a chair leg, in accordance with what is actually inside it. Nearly all the frustrations that drive beginners to blame their tools are misreadings. A plane that tears out chunks on one pass and leaves glass on the reverse pass is not blunt; it was being pushed against the fibres. A door that binds every winter was made from flat-sawn stock that moves twice as much as quartersawn would have. A chisel handle that snapped near the ferrule almost certainly had grain running out of its side. There is also an economic argument. Timber varies enormously in price by grade and figure, and grading rules are largely descriptions of grain features. Being able to look at a rough board in a yard and see where the clear cuttings are, whether the apparent flaw is a knot cluster or harmless bark inclusion, whether the shimmer on the face is genuine curl or just a planing artefact, is the difference between buying wood well and buying it badly. Rough-sawn stock hides most of this under saw marks and dirt, and a block plane or a wetted thumb applied to a small patch will usually reveal enough. The vocabulary is unfortunately loose. Grain is used by different trades to mean the direction of the fibres, the size of the pores, the pattern on a face, and the general texture, and figure is often used interchangeably with it. Precision helps: grain direction is where the fibres point in three dimensions; grain pattern or ring pattern is what the growth rings draw on a surface; texture is the size and uniformity of the cells; and figure is any distinctive optical or structural pattern beyond the plain ring layout. Almost every confusing piece of woodworking advice becomes clear once these four are kept apart.

sections.heading: Inside the Tree: Cells, Rings, Rays and Sap
sections.body: A tree grows outward from a thin sleeve of dividing cells called the cambium, which lies immediately under the bark. Each season the cambium lays down new wood, xylem, on its inner face and new bark, phloem, on its outer face. That is why a nail driven into a trunk stays at the same height for a century while the trunk thickens around it, and why removing a ring of bark all the way round kills the tree. In temperate climates growth is seasonal, and the wood laid down in spring differs from that laid down in summer. Earlywood, formed during the rush of spring growth, has large thin-walled cells built for conducting water; latewood, formed later, has smaller thick-walled cells and is denser and darker. The alternation produces annual growth rings. In tropical species with no marked dry season, rings may be faint or absent entirely, which is one reason mahogany and many tropical timbers look so uniform. Counting rings gives age, and the discipline of dendrochronology, founded by A. E. Douglass in the early twentieth century, uses the varying widths of those rings to date timbers to the exact year and to reconstruct past climate; a Bronze Age log and a modern tree from the same region can be cross-matched on ring-width patterns alone. Running at right angles to the rings, radiating from the centre like spokes, are the rays: ribbons of cells that store food and move it sideways. In most species they are microscopic. In oak they can be a centimetre or more deep, and it is these that produce the silver flecks or medullary figure prized in quartersawn oak furniture. Rays are also planes of weakness, which is why oak splits so cleanly along a radius and why radial checks in a drying log always open along a ray. Two zones make up the cross-section of most mature trunks. Sapwood, the outer band, is living, conducts water, is usually paler, and contains starches that insects and fungi eat readily. Heartwood, the inner core, is dead conducting tissue that the tree has plugged and impregnated with extractives, the compounds that give teak, cedar, black walnut and yew their colour, smell and natural decay resistance. The practical consequences are direct: sapwood is not durable outdoors regardless of species, so a fence post of untreated pine sapwood may fail in three years where the heartwood of the same log lasts fifteen, and the pale stripe on the edge of a walnut board is not a defect of colour only but a genuinely different material. Hardwood and softwood, finally, are botanical labels, not measures of hardness. Hardwoods are broadleaved flowering trees with vessels, or pores; softwoods are conifers without them. Balsa is a hardwood and yew is a softwood, and both facts embarrass the terminology annually.

sections.heading: Sawing Patterns: Flat-Sawn, Quartersawn and Rift
sections.body: A log is round and boards are flat, so every board is a compromise, and which compromise was chosen determines how the board looks, how it moves and how much it cost. The controlling variable is the angle between the growth rings and the wide face of the board, read off the end grain. Flat-sawn, also called plain-sawn or through-and-through, means the rings meet the face at less than about thirty degrees, and in the boards nearest the centre of the log they run almost parallel to it. This is the cheapest conversion because the log is simply sliced straight through with minimal handling and almost no waste. It produces the familiar cathedral or flame pattern, nested arches on the face, formed where the plane of the cut slices obliquely through the cone-shaped ring surfaces. Flat-sawn stock is also the least stable: it moves roughly twice as much in width as quartersawn, and because the rings try to straighten as they dry it cups away from the heart, so the face that was nearer the bark becomes concave. Quartersawn means the rings meet the face at sixty to ninety degrees, standing nearly on edge. The log is quartered first and each quarter sawn radially, which costs far more in labour and yields narrower boards with more waste. The face shows straight parallel lines rather than arches, and in ray-rich species such as oak, plane, beech and lacewood, the cut slices along the ray plane and produces flecks, sometimes covering the whole surface. Quartersawn boards move about half as much across their width, do not cup, wear more evenly on a floor, and take finish more uniformly. Their historical association with Arts and Crafts and Mission furniture is not just taste; Gustav Stickley's oak was quartersawn because it stayed flat. Rift-sawn sits between, at roughly thirty to sixty degrees, and is usually specified to get the straight line pattern without the ray fleck, which is why rift white oak is standard for table legs where four faces should match. The numbers are worth carrying. For a typical hardwood moving between about seven and twelve per cent moisture content, tangential shrinkage runs around eight per cent of dimension, radial about four, and longitudinal about one tenth of one per cent. A 300 mm wide flat-sawn oak panel can therefore change width by five or six millimetres between a damp summer and a heated winter, while its length changes by a fraction of a millimetre. Every frame and panel door, breadboard end and buttoned tabletop in the history of furniture exists to accommodate that single asymmetry. Reading which conversion you have takes two seconds: look at the end grain and judge the ring angle, and if the rings arch across the end like a rainbow the board will cup away from that arch as it dries.

sections.heading: Grain Direction in Three Dimensions
sections.body: The single most useful mental model is to picture a board as a bundle of drinking straws glued side by side, then to accept that the bundle is almost never perfectly parallel to the board's edges. Grain direction is a three-dimensional fact and has to be read on more than one surface. On the end grain you see the straws in cross-section, and this tells you the sawing pattern and how the board will move. On the face and edges you see them in length, and this tells you which way to cut, plane and feed. The critical thing the face reveals is slope of grain: the angle between the fibres and the long axis of the board. A board sawn from a straight, vertically grown log has fibres nearly parallel to its edges. A board sawn from a leaning tree, a tapering butt log, or one sawn to a line that was not parallel to the pith, has fibres that run diagonally, and where a fibre reaches the surface and stops, that is runout. Slope of grain is measured as a ratio and it is worth learning to express it that way, because every strength rule uses it. If the fibres deviate by 25 mm over 300 mm of length, that is a slope of 1 in 12. Structural grading rules typically demand 1 in 10 or better for general framing, 1 in 12 to 1 in 15 for higher grades, and traditional practice for tool handles and ladder rails is 1 in 15 or straighter. Strength falls off far faster than intuition suggests: an approximation known as the Hankinson formula predicts that tensile strength at 1 in 10 is already down to roughly half the straight-grained value, and at 1 in 5 to something like a quarter, because the load starts being carried by the weak glue between fibres rather than by the fibres themselves. Reading direction on a planed face is a learned trick with three reliable methods. First, look at the edge of the board rather than the face: on a quartersawn or rift edge the fibre lines emerge at a shallow angle, and they point the way a plane should travel, uphill in the sense that you cut with the lie of the fibres rather than lifting them. Second, run a thumbnail or fingertip lightly along the surface in both directions; one direction feels smooth and the other slightly rough, and the smooth one is with the grain. Third, take a light test cut with a sharp plane at each end; the direction that leaves a shaving and a bright surface is right, the one that tears fibres out is wrong. For flat-sawn faces the cathedral arches give a further clue. The arches point like nested arrowheads, and planing in the direction the arches point, from the open ends of the arches toward their peaks, is usually correct. It is genuinely only a rule of thumb, because the arch pattern is a section through a cone and the fibre direction underneath does not always agree with it.

sections.heading: Runout: What It Is, How To See It, Why It Breaks Things
sections.body: Runout is the condition where fibres that were continuous inside the tree have been severed by the saw and now run out of the face or edge of a board. Look closely at any sawn face and you will see fibres that begin somewhere in the middle of it, taper and disappear: each of those is a fibre that was cut across rather than followed. Runout is not damage and not a defect of the tree. It is a consequence of making a straight cut through a material whose fibres were not straight. It matters because wood carries load along its fibres and hardly at all between them. The lignin and hemicellulose that bond adjacent cells are perhaps a twentieth as strong in tension as the cellulose chains running along them. A piece with continuous fibres from end to end behaves like a rope. A piece with severe runout behaves like a rope that has been cut most of the way through at an angle, and it will fail along the interface without warning at a fraction of the expected load. This is why a shop-bought hammer handle can snap in a season while a riven ash handle lasts three generations, and why the failure of a runout-crossed handle is sudden rather than gradual. Seeing runout takes practice but is not subtle once the eye has it. On a planed surface, look along the board at a low angle with a light source behind the far end; runout shows as fine hairlines or as short fibre ends catching the light. Bending the piece slightly and watching where the surface fibres tent up reveals it as well. The most reliable test is destructive and therefore reserved for offcuts: split a short sample with a froe or a chisel and see whether the split runs out to the side within a few centimetres. A split follows the fibres exactly, which is precisely what makes it a perfect indicator and also the reason riving exists. The strength requirement is only one half. The other is surface quality: runout is the direct cause of tearout in planing, because a blade meeting fibres that rise toward the surface lifts and levers them out ahead of the cut rather than severing them. It also causes ragged results in routing, ragged edges on sawn cuts, and blotchy stain because severed fibre ends absorb more finish than intact ones. The remedies form a hierarchy. Choose stock without severe runout for anything load-bearing, and reject rather than repair. Where runout is present and unavoidable, orient it so that it lies on a face in compression rather than tension, since compression across the fibre interface is far less dangerous. Reduce cutting angle problems with a high-angle or back-bevelled plane iron, a tight chipbreaker set a few tenths of a millimetre from the edge, or a scraper. And for handles, rungs, wedges, shingles and basket splints, do not saw at all: split the stock and let the wood choose the surface.

sections.heading: Riving and Splitting: Letting the Fibres Choose
sections.body: Riving is the deliberate splitting of green wood along its natural fibre planes, and it is the oldest conversion method there is, predating the saw by millennia. Its whole logic is that a split cannot cross fibres, so every riven surface is by definition a zero-runout surface. A riven billet has fibres continuous end to end even if the tree twisted, which is why handle, ladder, chair and basket makers all rive rather than saw. Green wood is very much easier to split than dry, typically requiring a third to a half the force, because the water plasticises the lignin and the fibres part rather than tearing. Ring-porous hardwoods split best: oak, ash, chestnut, hickory and hazel are the classic riving timbers. Interlocked-grain species such as elm barely split at all, which is why elm was chosen for wheel hubs and chair seats. The key technique is control of the split's path. A split naturally follows the thicker of the two sides, so it wanders toward the weaker half and can run off the end of a billet, wasting it. The fix is counter-intuitive: bend the thicker side. Levering the heavier half away from the split forces the crack back toward the middle, and that single manoeuvre is the whole craft of accurate riving. Because riven material works best green, the sequence is rive, shape wet with a drawknife, then season before final fitting.
ingredients: A straight, knot-free green log or bolt felled within a few weeks; oak, ash, sweet chestnut, hickory or hazel split most predictably.
A froe: an L-shaped blade 200 to 300 mm long with a handle at right angles, used as a steerable wedge rather than a cutting tool.
A club or maul of green wood, not a steel hammer, which would mushroom the froe's back.
Two or three steel or wooden wedges for starting splits in larger rounds.
A riving brake: two forked stakes that grip the billet and leave both hands free to lever.
A drawknife and a shaving horse for shaping the blank while it is still green.
steps: Cut the log to length with 50 to 100 mm of waste at each end, and reject any bolt showing spiral grain or knots within that length.
Stand the round on a solid block and start a split across the full diameter with a wedge and maul until it opens into halves.
Halve each half again, always into two equal parts rather than shaving off a slice; splitting off-centre almost always runs out.
At arm thickness switch to the froe: set the blade across the end grain, strike until it bites 30 mm, then stop hitting it.
Lever the handle sideways to propagate the split by wedging, walking the froe down into the crack as it opens.
The moment the split favours one side, hold the thicker half and bend it away; the crack steers back toward the centre.
Shape green and slightly oversize, then sticker the parts with 20 mm air gaps in shade for about a year per 25 mm of thickness.

sections.heading: Figure: What Makes a Board Beautiful
sections.body: Figure is any distinctive pattern on a wood surface beyond the plain layout of growth rings, and almost all of it is optical rather than pigmentary. The underlying physics is straightforward. Wood fibres act like bundles of tiny optical fibres; where they are cut at an angle, their exposed ends reflect light back toward a viewer differently from fibres lying flat. When the fibre direction undulates, some regions present ends and some present sides, and the pattern of light and dark reverses as the viewer or the light moves. That shifting, three-dimensional shimmer is called chatoyance, from the French for cat's eye, and it is the reason a figured board photographs so poorly and looks so extraordinary in the hand. Curl, also called fiddleback or flame, comes from fibres that wave up and down in regular ripples perpendicular to the trunk axis, typically two to five waves per centimetre. Sliced across, the alternating end-on and side-on regions produce the familiar bands. Its cause is not fully settled; genetics, growth stress and site conditions all appear to contribute, and it cannot be reliably predicted from a standing tree, which is part of why it commands a premium. Maple, sycamore, ash and cherry show it most often, and the violin trade's demand for it goes back to the sixteenth century. Quilt is a larger-scale, blistered, three-dimensional bubbling most famous in bigleaf maple, produced by broad undulations in the fibre. Birdseye is a scatter of small conical dimples, best known in hard maple, whose cause remains genuinely disputed; theories include dormant bud traces, localised nutrient or hormonal disturbance, and fungal or insect involvement, and no one has yet grown it to order. Burl or burr is a chaotic mass of dormant buds and distorted grain forming a tumour-like growth on a trunk, producing dense clusters of eyes and swirls with essentially no consistent fibre direction, which makes it beautiful, unstable and prone to falling apart under a plane. Crotch or feather figure occurs where a trunk forks and the two sets of fibres interweave under compression, giving the plume seen in walnut and mahogany. Ray fleck, in quartersawn oak and plane, is structural rather than undulatory, being the ray tissue exposed in its own plane. Pommele, ribbon and roey stripe in mahogany, sapele and other tropical species come from interlocked grain, where the tree reverses its spiral direction every few years, so alternate bands face opposite ways and the stripe flips as you walk past it. Spalting is a different phenomenon entirely: the black zone lines are fungal barriers laid down where competing colonies meet in decaying wood. It is decay caught at a useful stage, which means spalted stock is weakened, sometimes punky, and carries spores worth respecting with a mask.

sections.heading: Pores, Texture and Species Identification by Eye
sections.body: Identifying a timber from a small planed sample is a genuine skill, and the reliable route is not colour, which varies wildly with age, light exposure and finish, but the arrangement of pores seen on the end grain. A hand lens of ten to fourteen times magnification and a freshly sliced end-grain surface, pared with a sharp chisel or razor rather than sanded, will settle most questions in under a minute. Hardwoods fall into three groups by pore distribution. Ring-porous species produce a band of large earlywood vessels at the start of each ring and much smaller latewood vessels afterwards, giving a strong visual ring boundary and a coarse, open texture on the face. Oak, ash, elm, chestnut and hickory are ring-porous, and this is why their long open pores hold dirt, need grain filler for a mirror finish, and make them terrible choices for a wine cup unless coopered. Diffuse-porous species scatter vessels evenly through the ring, producing faint boundaries and an even, fine texture. Maple, birch, cherry, poplar, beech and most tropical hardwoods are diffuse-porous, take detail crisply, and finish smooth without filler. Semi-ring-porous species such as walnut and some cherries sit between the two. Softwoods have no vessels at all, only tracheids, so the end grain shows no pores under a lens, just the earlywood-to-latewood density change. The presence or absence of resin canals is the next discriminator: pines, spruces, larches and Douglas fir have them, appearing as small dark specks, while firs, cedars, hemlocks and yew do not. Combined with smell, which is a legitimate diagnostic, cedar, cypress and pine are unmistakable on a fresh cut, this narrows most softwoods quickly. Other usable characters include weight, since density is one of the strongest predictors of behaviour and a small offcut in the hand tells you a great deal; hardness, testable by pressing a thumbnail into a corner; ray height, visible on the end grain as fine lines crossing the rings; and the presence of tyloses, the bubble-like plugs filling the earlywood vessels of white oak but not red oak, which is why white oak is watertight enough for barrels and red oak is not. Blowing gently through a short piece of red oak end-to-end will actually pass air; white oak will not, and this parlour trick is a genuinely definitive test. Two honest cautions. Positive identification to species is often impossible by eye even for specialists, since many timbers are sold under trade names covering several botanical species with different properties. And endangered or restricted timbers, particularly rosewoods and ebonies under CITES regulation, cannot be distinguished from legal substitutes without laboratory work, so provenance paperwork matters more than appearance.

sections.heading: Grain Direction and Machining: Tearout and How To Beat It
sections.body: Tearout is the lifting and levering-out of fibres ahead of a cutting edge, and understanding it converts a maddening surface defect into a controllable variable. When a blade meets fibres that slope up toward the surface, the wedge action of the bevel lifts them, and because wood splits far more easily than it shears, the split runs ahead of the edge and a chunk of fibre tears free below the intended surface. The depth of the damage is roughly proportional to how far the split runs before the edge catches up. Four levers control it, and they can be applied in any combination. The first is direction: cut with the fibres wherever the geometry allows, and simply reversing a board on a jointer or reversing the direction of a hand plane pass solves the majority of cases. Where grain reverses within one board, which is routine in figured stock, direction alone cannot save you. The second is cutting angle. A standard bench plane with a 45-degree bed produces a shaving that lifts and levers. Raising the effective attack angle to 50, 55 or 60 degrees changes the mechanism from splitting to scraping, at the cost of more effort and faster edge dulling. This is achieved by a high-angle frog, a bevel-up plane with a steep blade bevel, or, most cheaply, by honing a small back bevel of 10 to 15 degrees on an ordinary iron. At around 90 degrees you have a scraper, which cannot tear out at all and produces dust and fine shavings rather than continuous ones. The third is chip control. A chipbreaker set very close to the edge, on the order of 0.1 to 0.3 mm, bends the shaving sharply upward the instant it forms and stops the split running ahead. Research at the University of Tokyo in the 1980s, later publicised widely in the 2010s, demonstrated this experimentally with high-speed film, confirming what nineteenth-century plane makers had asserted. On machines the equivalent is a chip breaker bar and pressure bar on a planer or thicknesser, and closing the throat opening of a hand plane serves the same purpose less effectively. The fourth is depth of cut and moisture. Halving the shaving thickness roughly halves the leverage available to lift a fibre, so a series of fine passes beats one heavy one. Lightly dampening a difficult surface with a wiped film of water or alcohol a minute before planing softens the fibres and reliably improves the result, at the cost of raised grain that must be dealt with afterwards. Sharpness underlies all four: a dull edge does not sever, it pushes, and pushing is exactly what tears.

sections.heading: Movement: Why Wood Shrinks, Swells and Cups
sections.body: Wood is hygroscopic: it exchanges water with the surrounding air until it reaches equilibrium moisture content, and it changes dimension while doing so, permanently and forever. No finish stops this; a good film finish merely slows the exchange so that a piece responds to the season rather than to the weather. Understanding movement is not optional, because it is the single largest cause of furniture failure. Water sits in wood in two places. Free water fills the cell cavities, and losing it causes no dimensional change at all. Bound water sits within the cell walls, chemically associated with the cellulose, and losing it makes the walls themselves shrink. The changeover happens at the fibre saturation point, around 28 to 30 per cent moisture content for most species. Above that, drying costs weight but not size; below it, every further percentage point costs dimension, roughly linearly. Equilibrium moisture content depends on relative humidity and, weakly, on temperature. Useful anchor values: about 6 per cent at 30 per cent relative humidity, about 9 per cent at 50 per cent, about 12 per cent at 65 per cent, about 16 per cent at 80 per cent. A heated house in a cold winter can sit at 25 to 30 per cent relative humidity, while the same room in a humid summer reaches 70 per cent, so interior furniture typically cycles between roughly 6 and 12 per cent moisture content every year. The anisotropy is the crux. Shrinkage from green to oven-dry runs about 0.1 to 0.2 per cent along the grain, 3 to 6 per cent radially, and 6 to 12 per cent tangentially, with tangential typically about twice radial. That two-to-one ratio explains almost every drying defect. A flat-sawn board cups because its outer face, closer to tangential, shrinks more than its inner face. A round log checks radially because the circumference wants to shrink more than the radius allows. A square section cut off-centre becomes a diamond. A round dowel dries oval. And a board that dries too fast case-hardens: the shell dries and sets in tension while the core is still wet, so when the core finally shrinks, the piece cups violently or pinches the saw when ripped. The design responses are few and ancient. Allow cross-grain movement rather than resisting it: floating panels in grooved frames, tabletops fixed with buttons or slotted screws, breadboard ends pinned only at the centre with elongated holes elsewhere. Never glue a long cross-grain joint. Acclimatise stock in the room where it will live for at least a week, and preferably several. And balance construction, finishing both faces of a panel equally, so that neither face exchanges moisture faster than the other.

sections.heading: Grain and Joinery: Where Strength Actually Lives
sections.body: Every wood joint is an argument about grain direction, and joints fail almost exclusively where that argument was lost. Two facts govern the whole subject. First, a glue bond between two long-grain surfaces is stronger than the wood itself, so a properly made edge joint in a panel will break beside the glue line rather than along it. Second, a glue bond to end grain is worth perhaps ten to twenty per cent of that, because the exposed cell ends behave like a bundle of straws that wick adhesive away from the interface and offer almost no surface for bonding. This is the entire explanation for traditional joinery. A mortise and tenon exists to convert an end-grain butt into long-grain glue surface: the tenon cheeks meet the mortise walls long grain to long grain, and the joint's shoulders resist racking. A dovetail exists because its geometry resists withdrawal mechanically, so even if the glue on the end-grain portions contributes little, the wood itself locks. A bridle joint, half-lap, finger joint and biscuit all do the same job of manufacturing long-grain contact area where a butt joint offered none. Modern pocket screws and dominoes are the same idea executed differently. Grain direction also determines where a part will break. Short grain, meaning a small region where fibres run across rather than along a narrow section, is a guaranteed failure point. It appears most often in curved parts sawn from straight boards: cut a chair's curved back leg from a plank and somewhere along the curve the fibres will run out across a narrow section, and that is where it will snap. The traditional solutions are to steam-bend, which keeps fibres continuous through the curve, to laminate thin strips that each follow the curve, or to select naturally curved stock, which is why shipwrights and wheelwrights sought grown crooks and compass timber and paid a premium for them. Cross-grain construction is the other classic error. Gluing a solid batten across the width of a solid panel constrains a member that will move six millimetres against one that will move a tenth of that, and the result is a split panel or a failed glue line within a couple of seasons, guaranteed. The correct detail is to allow sliding: a sliding dovetail glued only at the front, or screws through slotted holes. Plywood and other engineered boards sidestep this entirely by alternating ply direction so that movement is mutually restrained, which is exactly why a plywood cabinet back can be glued into a rebate while a solid one cannot. The practical audit before glue-up is to name, for every joint, which two surfaces are long grain to long grain and which member is free to move in width. A joint that cannot answer both questions is a joint that will fail, and it is far cheaper to find that out with a pencil than in a customer's dining room three winters later.

sections.heading: Bending, Steaming and Laminating Along the Grain
sections.body: Bending wood exploits the fact that its two faces are doing different jobs: the outside of a curve is in tension, the inside in compression. Wood is exceptionally strong in tension along the grain but yields in compression at a much lower stress, buckling its cell walls into small folds. That asymmetry is the whole basis of steam bending. Heat and moisture soften the lignin, the polymer that stiffens the cell walls, which becomes rubbery at roughly 80 degrees Celsius when wet. The wood can then be shortened on the inside of the curve by perhaps 25 to 30 per cent, while being stretched on the outside by only one or two per cent before it fails. The practical consequence is counter-intuitive and is the single most important fact in the craft: a steam bend succeeds by compressing the inside, not by stretching the outside. That is why a metal compression strap with fixed end stops is essential for anything beyond a gentle curve. The strap takes the tensile load entirely, forcing all the deformation into compression, and a bend that fractures without one will usually succeed with one. Selection dominates outcome. Air-dried or green stock at 20 to 30 per cent moisture content bends; kiln- dried stock at 8 per cent largely does not, because kilning permanently cross-links some of the lignin. Straight-grained, runout-free riven stock bends; sawn stock with a slope of grain steeper than about 1 in 15 fails at the runout. Ring-porous hardwoods bend best, with ash, oak, beech, elm, hickory and walnut the classic choices, while most softwoods and many tropical hardwoods bend badly or not at all. Knots, even small ones, are reliable failure points. Steaming time is roughly 45 minutes to an hour per 25 mm of thickness at atmospheric pressure and about 100 degrees Celsius, and over-steaming does no good and eventually weakens the piece. Once out of the box, working time is short, on the order of 30 to 60 seconds, because the wood stiffens as it cools, so the form and clamps must be ready and rehearsed. The bent piece must then be held on the form until dry, typically several days to weeks, and it will still spring back a few per cent, so forms are usually cut slightly tighter than the target radius. Lamination is the alternative and is more predictable, if less romantic. Thin strips, each flexible enough to bend elastically without steam, are glued and clamped over a form. Because each layer is thin, the strain in each is small, and the cured glue lines lock the assembly into shape with very little springback. A urea-formaldehyde or epoxy glue resists creep far better than PVA, which can allow a laminated curve to relax over years. Kerf bending, sawing repeated slots partway through the inside face, is a third method, structurally weak and used mainly where the bend will be hidden or supported.

sections.heading: Reaction Wood, Knots and Other Growth Features
sections.body: Trees respond to being pushed out of vertical by growing corrective tissue, and this reaction wood is one of the most troublesome things a woodworker can encounter, largely because it is easy to miss until the timber is cut and starts moving. Conifers form compression wood on the underside of a lean or a branch, pushing the stem back upright. It is denser, darker and duller than normal wood, has abnormally wide latewood bands making the rings look eccentric, and shrinks longitudinally by up to ten times the normal amount, sometimes exceeding one per cent. A board containing a streak of it will bow dramatically as it dries and will keep moving. Broadleaved trees form tension wood on the upper side, pulling the stem up. It is often paler and has a woolly, fuzzy surface that will not plane or sand cleanly, and it also shrinks abnormally along the grain. Both types are found in leaning trees, in branch wood, and in the butt logs of trees grown on slopes or at the edge of a stand, which is a good reason to be suspicious of very cheap stock from thinnings. Knots are the bases of branches embedded in the trunk, and their significance depends on whether the branch was alive when the wood grew round it. A live or intergrown knot is continuous with the surrounding tissue and stays put. A dead or encased knot is surrounded by bark and is not attached; it becomes a loose knot that falls out and leaves a hole. Either way the fibres of the trunk deviate around a knot exactly as water flows round a stone, producing local grain distortion, tearout and a strength reduction that can be substantial. Structural grading rules limit knots by size and, importantly, by position: a knot at the edge of a beam in tension matters far more than one at the neutral axis. Several other features are worth naming. Spiral grain, where fibres wind helically round the trunk, produces boards that twist as they dry and is invisible on a planed face but obvious in the bark's pattern on a standing tree. Interlocked grain, where the spiral reverses every few years, produces the ribbon stripe of sapele and makes planing in any single direction impossible. Shakes are separations along the growth rings, ring shake following a ring and star shake radiating from the centre, and both often stem from wind or felling damage. Checks are surface splits from drying too fast. Included bark, where two stems grew together with bark trapped between, creates a plane with no strength at all, frequently at the crotch that also produces the prettiest figure.

sections.heading: Choosing and Laying Out Stock for a Project
sections.body: Layout is where reading grain turns into decisions, and it is worth more attention than most people give it, because a good layout costs nothing but ten minutes and cannot be recovered later. The sequence used in traditional shops is deliberate and worth following. Begin by sorting the whole pile before cutting anything. Sight down each board's length and edge for bow, crook, cup and twist, mark defects in chalk, and note the ring orientation on each end. Wet a small patch with mineral spirits or water to reveal figure and colour that rough sawing hides. Then assign roles. Show faces, tops, doors, drawer fronts, get the best figure and colour match, ideally from a single board so that grain runs continuously across the piece. Structural parts, legs, rails, stretchers, get the straightest grain regardless of appearance, because slope of grain governs their strength. Secondary parts, drawer sides, backs, bottoms, take whatever remains. Cut long parts first, then short: the reverse order strands you with pieces too short for the rails. Leave generous allowance, at least 25 mm on length and 3 to 6 mm on width and thickness, and rough-cut oversize a day or two before final milling so that internal stress can release before you flatten. This single habit, rough-mill, wait, then finish-mill, eliminates the majority of parts that mysteriously bow overnight. For legs and any four-sided part, orient stock so the visible faces show consistent grain, which normally means rift-sawn material with rings running diagonally so all four faces read similarly. For a panel glued from several boards, alternate the ring orientation if you fear cupping in a wide unrestrained panel, but if the panel will be held flat in a frame it is better to ignore ring direction and match grain and colour instead, since appearance is the thing you cannot fix later. Grain should run in a consistent direction along a panel so it can all be planed the same way; a reversed board in the middle of a top will haunt every finishing session. Mark parts as soon as they are cut, using a cabinetmaker's triangle across the assembled faces so that orientation, face side and face edge are recoverable after the pieces are separated and shuffled. Mark the face side and face edge with the traditional pencil loop and tick, and make every subsequent measurement from those two reference surfaces rather than from opposite faces, which will not be perfectly parallel. Finally, record grain direction with a light arrow on the waste or the hidden face; it saves rediscovering it at every machine and is the cheapest insurance against tearout on a part that is already nearly finished.

sections.heading: Diagnosing Problems: What Went Wrong and Why
sections.body: Most workshop faults have a small number of grain-related causes, and diagnosing by symptom is faster than guessing at tools. A surface that tears out in patches, especially in figured stock, is a grain-direction and cutting-angle problem, not a sharpening one, though a dull edge makes everything worse. Reverse direction, raise the effective cutting angle, close the chipbreaker, take a lighter cut, or move to a scraper. A surface that looks fine dry but shows a blotchy patchwork under finish is usually differential absorption caused by runout and by density variation; the remedy is a wash coat of dilute shellac or a purpose-made conditioner before stain, applied to a test offcut first. A board that cupped after milling was flat-sawn and lost moisture unevenly, most often because it was stacked on a bench with one face exposed and the other against wood. Sticker everything with air on both faces. A board that bowed along its length after ripping had internal stress, either case-hardening from fast kilning or reaction wood; a rip that closes on the blade and pinches, or one that springs open by several millimetres, is the diagnostic sign. Take such stock down in stages, alternating faces, and expect to lose thickness. A panel that split along a glue line in the first winter was almost certainly restrained across the grain, by a glued batten, a screw in a round hole through a wide top, or a panel glued into its frame grooves. The wood will always win that argument. A tabletop that stayed flat but pulled its buttons out was allowed to move but not far enough; slots need travel proportional to width, roughly one millimetre per hundred millimetres of panel width in each direction for interior work in a temperate climate. A handle, rung or curved leg that snapped cleanly at an angle across its width failed at runout. There is no repair worth making; make the part again from riven or naturally curved stock, and take the failure as information about the whole batch. A steam bend that fractured on the outside of the curve was bent without a compression strap, from kiln-dried stock, or from a piece with a knot or runout at the apex. Finally, if a project fights you at every stage, planes badly, moves overnight, will not stay square, the likeliest single explanation is that the timber was not at equilibrium with the workshop when work began. Bring stock indoors, sticker it, and leave it a fortnight before cutting. It is the least glamorous intervention in woodworking and by a wide margin the most effective. A cheap pin-type moisture meter, costing very little, will confirm in seconds what a fortnight of guessing cannot, and reading two boards from the same pile against each other is often more informative than either absolute figure.

guides.safetyNote: Grain direction governs strength: a handle, rung or chair leg with more than about 1 in 15 slope of grain can fail suddenly under load, without warning and often at full force. Never use a runout-crossed piece for a hammer handle, ladder rail, climbing hold, tool handle or any component that would injure someone if it snapped. Riving or splitting stock follows the fibres and is far safer than sawing for these parts. Reaction wood and freshly milled boards can also move violently or pinch a blade as internal stress releases; use a riving knife on a table saw, stand out of the kickback line, and rip suspect stock in stages, letting it move between passes.

guides.title: Choosing Hardwoods for Furniture Projects
guides.summary: A comprehensive guide to selecting hardwood lumber for furniture, covering wood anatomy, density and hardness, moisture movement, sawing patterns, strength, workability, the major temperate and tropical species, grading and buying, and the failure modes that ruin finished work.

sections.heading: Why the Choice of Wood Decides a Project's Fate
sections.body:
Every piece of furniture is an argument between a designer and a material that was never grown to be furniture. A tree builds wood to hold a crown of leaves against wind and gravity, to carry water upward under tension, and to resist fungi and insects long enough to reproduce. None of those purposes involve staying flat, taking a mirror finish, or holding a mortise-and-tenon joint tight for two hundred years. When a woodworker picks a species and a board, they are deciding in advance how much the piece will move with the seasons, how heavy it will be to lift, whether the joints will crush or split, how the surface will take colour, and whether the thing will still be sound when the maker is long dead. Almost every catastrophic furniture failure that is not simply bad joinery traces back to a wood choice made without understanding what that wood does.

The stakes are not merely aesthetic. A twenty-four-inch-wide tabletop in flatsawn hard maple, glued rigidly to an apron across the grain, will generate enough force in a dry winter to tear itself apart; the same top in the same species, fastened with slotted buttons that let it slide, will survive indefinitely. A chair leg cut from straight-grained white ash will bend and spring back under a person rocking on the back legs; the identical leg in short-grained tropical padauk or in a piece of oak with the grain running out the side may snap without warning. A cutting board in red oak will wick liquid straight through its open pores, while the same board in white oak, whose vessels are plugged by balloon-like growths called tyloses, is effectively watertight. These are not preferences. They are consequences of anatomy that can be predicted before a single cut is made.

Wood selection also encodes cost, availability and ethics. A cubic foot of black walnut may cost eight or ten times a cubic foot of yellow poplar in the same market, and a rosewood that looked merely expensive in 1970 is now a regulated species whose international trade is restricted by treaty. Choosing well means holding several questions at once: what mechanical and dimensional behaviour does this part need, what visual character does the design want, what can be bought locally and legally at a price the project can bear, and what will the wood do to the tools and the finish along the way. A maker who understands the underlying mechanisms can answer all four from first principles rather than from a list of species memorised from a magazine, and can substitute intelligently when the intended wood is unavailable, which in practice is most of the time.

sections.heading: What Actually Makes a Wood a Hardwood
sections.body:
The word hardwood is one of the most misleading terms in the crafts, because it describes botany rather than hardness. Hardwoods are the woods of angiosperms, the flowering plants, which in temperate zones are usually broad-leaved and deciduous: oak, maple, cherry, ash, birch, walnut. Softwoods are the woods of gymnosperms, the cone-bearing conifers: pine, spruce, fir, larch, cedar, yew. The division is roughly 140 million years old, dating to the emergence of flowering plants in the Cretaceous, and it corresponds to a genuine difference in cellular plumbing rather than to any measured property of the finished board. Balsa, at roughly 160 kilograms per cubic metre and soft enough to dent with a thumbnail, is a hardwood. Pacific yew, harder than many oaks, is a softwood. Longleaf pine outperforms basswood in nearly every mechanical test, and both labels remain correct.

The real difference is in how the tree moves water. Softwoods conduct sap through tracheids, long tapering cells perhaps three to five millimetres long and thirty micrometres across, which do double duty as both plumbing and structure. Water passes from one tracheid to the next through valve-like pits in the shared walls. The result is a relatively uniform wood, easy to plane, without visible pores. Hardwoods evolved a specialised conducting cell called a vessel element: short, wide, open-ended tubes stacked into continuous pipes that can be many metres long and, in a ring-porous oak, up to about 300 micrometres in diameter, wide enough to be clearly visible as pores on an end-grain surface. Because the vessels handle conduction, hardwoods can devote other cells, notably thick-walled fibres, purely to strength. That division of labour is why hardwoods span such an enormous density range and why they produce so much more visual variety.

For a furniture maker the practical consequence is that hardwood pore structure sorts species into three working groups. Ring-porous woods such as red oak, white oak, ash, elm, chestnut and hickory produce a band of very large earlywood vessels at the start of each growing season, then much denser latewood. That contrast gives strong figure, coarse open texture that needs grain filler for a glass-smooth finish, and a tendency for the soft earlywood to crush under a chisel. Diffuse-porous woods such as maple, cherry, birch, beech, poplar, walnut and most tropical species scatter small vessels evenly through the ring, giving a fine, even texture that finishes smoothly straight off the plane. Semi-ring-porous woods, black walnut among them, sit between. Looking at the end grain of an unknown board with a hand lens and a freshly pared surface will place it in one of these groups within seconds, and that alone predicts a great deal about how it will cut, glue and finish.

sections.heading: Inside the Log: Heartwood, Sapwood, Rays and Grain
sections.body:
A cross-section of a mature trunk shows a layered history. At the centre is the pith, the original shoot, often only a few millimetres across and usually surrounded by juvenile wood: the first ten to twenty growth rings, which have lower density, more longitudinal shrinkage and a pronounced tendency to twist. Boards containing the pith or the wood immediately around it are a common source of unexplained warping and should be avoided for anything that must stay straight. Outside that lies the heartwood, wood whose living cells have died and which the tree has infused with extractives: phenols, tannins, resins, oils and pigments that give walnut its chocolate colour, cedar its aroma and white oak its rot resistance. Beyond the heartwood is a band of pale sapwood, still conducting water, still storing starch, and consequently attractive to fungi, powderpost beetles and mould. Heartwood and sapwood of the same tree have very nearly the same strength and shrinkage but very different colour and durability, which is why a walnut board with a cream-coloured stripe along one edge is a defect in a dining table and a design feature in a live-edge slab.

Radiating outward from the pith are the rays, ribbons of cells running horizontally that store and move food sideways. In most species they are microscopically thin. In the oaks, sycamore, plane and beech they are conspicuous, and in white and red oak they can be an inch or more tall in the radial direction. Rays are the reason quartersawn oak shows the shimmering figure that Gustav Stickley built an aesthetic on, and they are also planes of relative weakness along which a board can split. Rays contribute to why wood shrinks so much less along the radius than around the circumference.

Grain and figure are separate ideas that are constantly confused. Grain refers to the direction and arrangement of the longitudinal cells. Straight grain runs parallel to the board's length; interlocked grain, common in mahogany and sapele, reverses direction every few rings and produces the striped ribbon figure that also makes the wood tear out under any plane blade not set very fine. Spiral, wavy and curly grain, and the chaotic grain of burl and crotch wood, all raise figure and lower predictability at the same time. Figure is the visual pattern the surface shows, produced by the interaction of grain, ray tissue, colour variation and how the log was cut.

The single most useful habit is to read the end grain of every board before buying it. The curve of the growth rings tells you where in the log the board came from, the pore pattern identifies the working group, the presence of pith warns of twist, and the ring spacing hints at growth rate and therefore, in ring-porous species, at density and strength.

sections.heading: Density, Hardness and the Janka Scale
sections.body:
Density is the master variable of wood technology. Almost every mechanical property a furniture maker cares about, strength in bending, stiffness, resistance to denting, screw-holding, and the amount of energy needed to cut it, correlates strongly with how much cell-wall substance is packed into a given volume. The cell wall material itself is close to constant across all species at roughly 1.5 grams per cubic centimetre; what varies is how much of the volume is wall and how much is empty lumen. Balsa is mostly air at a specific gravity near 0.16, basswood 0.37, yellow poplar 0.42, black cherry 0.50, black walnut 0.55, red oak and hard maple both about 0.63, shagbark hickory 0.72, and ipe above 1.00, which is why ipe sinks in water.

The standard number quoted for hardness is the Janka rating, devised by the Austrian-born researcher Gabriel Janka around 1906 and later standardised. A steel ball 11.28 millimetres in diameter, chosen because its equatorial cross-section is exactly one square centimetre, is pressed into the wood until it is embedded to half its diameter, and the force required is recorded, in pounds-force in North American tables and in newtons elsewhere. Representative side-hardness figures for kiln-dried temperate species are basswood about 410 pounds-force, yellow poplar 540, butternut 490, black cherry 950, black walnut 1010, soft maple around 950 to 1100, yellow birch 1260, red oak 1290, ash 1320, white oak 1360, hard maple 1450 and hickory 1820. Tropical species climb far higher: teak sits at a modest 1070 despite its reputation, Honduran mahogany about 800, jatoba 2350, cumaru 3540 and ipe near 3680.

Two cautions matter. First, Janka is a surface property measured perpendicular to the grain; it predicts dent resistance in a tabletop or a floor and says almost nothing about stiffness in a long rail or splitting resistance in a thin leg. A very hard wood can still be brittle. Second, the numbers are averages over a natural material with enormous variation; two boards of red oak can easily differ by twenty per cent, and moisture content shifts hardness substantially, with dry wood testing considerably harder than green.

For selection, density buys dent resistance and strength but costs weight, tool wear and difficulty. A chest of drawers in hard maple will be genuinely heavy to move, will blunt hand-plane irons faster, and will burn under a dull router bit; the same carcase in cherry is easier in every operation and slightly softer in service. The right question is never which wood is hardest, but which is hard enough for how this surface will actually be used, while remaining light enough and workable enough for the person making it.

sections.heading: Moisture, Movement and Equilibrium Moisture Content
sections.body:
Wood is hygroscopic: it exchanges water vapour with the surrounding air until it reaches an equilibrium moisture content, or EMC, determined mainly by relative humidity and slightly by temperature. This exchange never stops. A finished dining table is not a stable object; it is a slow-breathing one, and virtually every crack, cupped panel and split tabletop in the world is the result of a maker who designed as though it were not.

The mechanism has a threshold. Freshly felled wood may hold water at 60 to 200 per cent of its oven-dry weight, most of it free water sitting in the cell cavities. As the wood dries, that free water leaves first and the wood does not shrink at all. Only when the cavities are empty and the water bound within the cell walls begins to leave does the wood start to move. That transition, the fibre saturation point, sits near 28 to 30 per cent moisture content in nearly all species. Below it, shrinkage is roughly linear with moisture content, so a board that has dried from 30 per cent to 6 per cent has done about eighty per cent of the shrinking it will ever do.

Indoor EMC in a heated temperate house typically runs 5 to 7 per cent in winter and 9 to 12 per cent in a humid summer; an unheated shed might sit at 12 to 15 per cent year-round, and a desert interior can drop below 4. Furniture lumber is kiln dried to 6 to 8 per cent because that brackets the interior average. Wood bought at 12 per cent and worked immediately will shrink after assembly, opening joints and cracking panels, so boards should be stickered flat in the room where the piece will live for one to three weeks before machining, and ideally checked with a resistance or pinless moisture meter.

Shrinkage is strongly anisotropic, and this is the fact that governs furniture design. Longitudinal shrinkage along the grain is negligible, typically 0.1 to 0.2 per cent, which is why a table leg never gets shorter. Radial shrinkage, along the rays from pith to bark, is moderate. Tangential shrinkage, around the growth rings, is roughly twice radial. Published green-to-ovendry figures include red oak 4.0 per cent radial and 8.6 tangential, white oak 5.6 and 10.5, hard maple 4.8 and 9.9, black cherry 3.7 and 7.1, black walnut 5.5 and 7.8, Honduran mahogany 3.7 and 5.1, and teak 2.6 and 5.8.

Turning that into a working number is simple arithmetic. Divide the green-to-ovendry percentage by thirty to get movement per one per cent change in moisture content. Red oak tangential gives 8.6 divided by 30, or 0.287 per cent per point. A 24-inch-wide flatsawn red oak top swinging four points, from 6 per cent in February to 10 per cent in August, moves 0.287 per cent times four times 24 inches, which is 0.275 inches, better than a quarter of an inch. That is the gap a breadboard end must accommodate and the reason a top is never glued rigidly across the grain.

sections.heading: Flatsawn, Quartersawn and Riftsawn: How the Cut Changes the Board
sections.body:
How a log is broken down determines the angle at which the growth rings meet the board's face, and that angle controls appearance, movement and stability more than almost any other single decision. The terminology varies between trades and countries, but the geometry is unambiguous. In a flatsawn board, also called plainsawn or through-and-through, the growth rings meet the wide face at less than about 30 degrees, running nearly parallel to it. In a quartersawn board the rings meet the face at 60 to 90 degrees, close to perpendicular. Riftsawn sits between, roughly 30 to 60 degrees.

The consequences follow directly from anisotropic shrinkage. A flatsawn face is dominated by tangential movement, so it changes width the most, roughly twice as much as quartersawn. It also cups, because the tangential shrinkage on the face nearer the bark exceeds that on the face nearer the pith, so the board curls away from the heart, a rule of thumb woodworkers state as the growth rings trying to straighten out. Flatsawn faces show the familiar cathedral or flame figure, which many people find handsome and which is by far the cheapest to produce because the sawyer simply keeps slicing straight through the log with minimal handling.

A quartersawn board of the same species moves only about half as much across its width and has almost no tendency to cup. Working the earlier arithmetic in red oak: the same 24-inch top, quartersawn, uses the radial coefficient of 4.0 divided by 30, or 0.133 per cent per point, so a four-point swing gives 0.128 inches, roughly an eighth, against a quarter-inch for flatsawn. Quartersawn oak also exposes the tall rays as broad shimmering flecks, the ray fleck that defines Arts and Crafts furniture, and quartersawn sycamore and lacewood show the same effect even more dramatically. Quartersawn material wears better as flooring, holds paint better, and is markedly more stable in wide panels, doors and drawer sides.

The cost is yield and price. Producing quartersawn boards requires repeatedly rotating the log and taking cuts through the radius, generating narrower boards and more waste, and premiums of 30 to 100 per cent over flatsawn are normal. Riftsawn material, in which the rings run diagonally, avoids both cathedral figure and ray fleck and produces the straight uniform grain prized for table and chair legs; a rift leg looks the same on all four faces, which no flatsawn leg does.

Practical selection follows the part. Use quartersawn or riftsawn for anything long and thin that must stay straight, for wide panels that must stay flat, for drawer sides, and for legs where consistent appearance matters. Use flatsawn where figure is wanted, where the panel is narrow or free to move, and where budget rules. Mixing the two within one glued-up top is a common error, because the two halves will move by different amounts and the joint between them will telegraph.

sections.heading: Strength Properties That Actually Matter in Furniture
sections.body:
Furniture rarely fails because the wood was not strong enough in the abstract. It fails in specific modes at specific places, and the properties that predict those modes are not the ones people quote. Four numbers do most of the work.

Modulus of elasticity, or MOE, measures stiffness: how far a member deflects under load before it breaks. It governs whether a bookshelf sags, whether a long table rail bows under a leaning elbow, and whether a chair feels solid. Typical values for dry temperate hardwoods run from about 1.3 million pounds per square inch for basswood through 1.49 million for black cherry, 1.58 for yellow poplar, 1.68 for black walnut, 1.74 for white ash, and 1.82 to 1.83 million for red oak and hard maple, with hickory near 2.16 million. Deflection in a simply supported shelf varies with the cube of the span and inversely with the cube of the thickness, so doubling a shelf's thickness reduces sag eightfold while switching from cherry to hard maple gains only about 23 per cent. Geometry beats species almost every time; if a shelf sags, thicken it or add a stiffening lip rather than reaching for a denser wood.

Modulus of rupture, or MOR, is the bending stress at failure. Representative dry values are black cherry 12,300 psi, red oak 14,300, black walnut 14,600, white ash 15,000, hard maple 15,800 and hickory around 20,000. Compression parallel to grain, which matters for legs and for the crushing of a tenon cheek, runs roughly 5,000 to 8,000 psi in these species. Compression perpendicular to grain is far lower, often only 800 to 1,500 psi, and it is why a clamp pad crushes a fibre or a chair rail dents where a bolt bears on it.

The property that quietly kills chairs is shear strength parallel to the grain, typically only 1,200 to 2,000 psi, roughly a tenth of bending strength. Wood splits along its length far more readily than it breaks across it. A short-grained leg, where the grain runs out through the side rather than along its length, has effectively no strength at all in that direction, because a load simply peels the fibres apart. This is why chair legs, especially cabriole legs sawn from a wide blank, must be laid out so the grain follows the length of the leg, and why through-tenons in end grain are a poor idea.
